docs.title: Zodiac
docs.text:
Zodiac is a desktop application for casting and studying horoscopes. It draws classical chart wheels, a planets view, and text tables; it works in both the tropical and sidereal zodiacs; and it reaches well beyond a typical charting program into harmonics, parans, primary directions, and a fast, pattern-driven event engine for transits and directions.

This site is the built-in help. You can reach it any time from inside the program by pressing F1 or clicking Help, and you can also read it online.

the main window — database tree on the left, chart wheel in the centre, the Events panel on the right

docs.title: What Zodiac does
docs.text:
At its simplest, you enter a date, time, and place and Zodiac draws the chart. From there the program opens up in several directions:

  • Multiple views of the same chart — a classical wheel, a planets view, and text tables, each kept in sync as you change display options.
  • Tropical and sidereal — the tropical zodiac plus three sidereal options: a non-equal "constellational" ayanamsha, and the two equal-sign 30° ayanamshas, Fagan–Bradley (Aldebaran fixed at 15° Taurus, favoured by Western siderealists) and Lahiri (Spica at 0° Libra, standard in Jyotish).
  • Nine house systems and over forty aspects, with adjustable orbs and filtering.
  • Harmonics from H1 to H32, shown dynamically on the wheel and explored in a dedicated Harmonics tab — including "overtones", so you can see the H4 pattern inside an H9 chart, or vice-versa.
  • Fixed stars, midpoints, and multiple coordinate frames — ecliptic, prime vertical, equatorial, and great-circle aspects.
  • Parans and primary directions — paranatellonta event finding, an interactive speculum, and several quotidian direction methods.
  • A fast event engine — transits-to-transits, transits-to-natal, progressions, stations, ingresses, returns, and heliacal apparitions, searchable with a compact pattern language.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Most of Zodiac's power is reached not by casting a new chart for every question, but by navigating through time and through a chart's features from tables — the events table, the speculum, the harmonics table, the directions tables. Rather than manually building a return chart, or a progressed chart, or hunting for the moment an aspect is exact, you set a range and let the tables find the moments for you; clicking a row brings up the corresponding chart. The program is, at heart, chart- and table-based, and that is the quickest way to get comfortable with it.

The interface is compact and dock-based, and you can arrange the toolbars and tables where you like. It may feel a little quirky if you are used to a commercial package, but the underlying model is simple.

docs.title: A note on this program's heritage
docs.text: Zodiac began as an open-source project by Artem Vasilev. Josh Baudhuin found it on SourceForge in 2015 — a clean, Qt-based, Swiss-Ephemeris charting program with a nice dark theme, aspect sets, a planetary-strength scoring system, and a simple chart database — and began adding features for western-sidereal and harmonic work. When the original author stepped back from the project, that work became this independent sidereal branch, developed since then to add sidereal ayanamshas, harmonic search, parans, primary directions, and the event engine. It is free software, built on the Swiss Ephemeris for its astronomical calculations.

docs.title: Getting help fast
docs.text: Inside the program, pressing F1 opens the page most relevant to whatever you are looking at — so F1 from the Events panel lands on the Events guide, not the top of the manual. If you prefer, the Help button and menu open this same site. Every page is searchable from the search box at the top.

docs.title: Chart Types
docs.text:
A natal chart is only the starting point. From that one set of birth data Zodiac derives a family of related charts — returns, progressions, composites, and bi-wheels — each of which answers a different question about time, development, or relationship.

The important thing to know is that you rarely have to hand-cast any of them. In the spirit of the program's table-based use model, the Events panel surfaces the moments these charts describe — the next solar return, a progressed contact, the exact hit of a transit — and clicking a row brings up the derived chart, often as chart #2 in a bi-wheel with the natal chart.

the Events panel with a return row selected on the left, and the resulting return chart drawn as a bi-wheel against the natal chart on the right

docs.title: The derived charts
docs.text:
• Returns — solar and sidereal returns, and (with a harmonic set) quarterly and demi-returns. They surface through the Events panel and feed primary-direction timing.
  • Progressions — secondary progressions, tracked as events both to the natal chart and to the progressions themselves.
  • Composite (midpoint) charts — a single chart synthesized from two people's charts by midpointing their positions.
  • Bi-wheels & synastry — overlaying a second chart on the natal chart to compare them, or to view transits and returns against the birth chart.

docs.title: Bi-Wheels & Synastry
docs.text:
A bi-wheel overlays a second chart on top of the natal chart (the radix), drawing the two side by side on one wheel so you can read them together. Zodiac highlights the key aspects between the two charts, which makes the bi-wheel the tool for two common jobs:

  • Synastry and comparison — placing one person's chart against another's to see how their planets aspect each other.
  • Transits and returns against the natal chart — laying a moment in time, or a return chart, over the birth chart to read the contacts it makes.

docs.title: Building a bi-wheel from events
docs.text:
The quickest way to get a bi-wheel is not to assemble one by hand. In the Events panel, clicking an event can make that moment chart #2 in a bi-wheel with the natal chart as chart #1 — so a transit, a return, or a progressed contact you found in the table appears immediately as an overlay on the radix, with its aspects to the birth chart drawn in.

a bi-wheel with a neutral natal demo chart as the inner wheel and a transit or return chart as the outer wheel, with the inter-chart aspect lines highlighted

docs.title: Prime-vertical bi-wheels
docs.text: The bi-wheel has a prime-vertical (mundoscope) mode in which both charts are coordinated in the same reference frame, so their positions can be compared correctly rather than each drawn in its own frame. This mode is especially useful for seeing angular coincidences — for example, when inspecting parans. How the coordinate frames work, and when to switch to prime vertical, is covered in Prime vertical, equatorial & great-circle.

docs.title: More than just the wheel
docs.text: A bi-wheel is not limited to the drawn chart. The Harmonics tab operates on bi-wheels too — clicking a harmonic or midpoint redraws the aspects across both charts — and the primary directions and PSSR tables can likewise be produced for the second chart in a bi-wheel, optionally including the natal planets (see Primary directions & quotidian modes).

docs.title: Composite (Midpoint) Charts
docs.text: A composite chart is a single chart that represents a relationship rather than a person. Instead of overlaying two charts to compare them — the job of a bi-wheel — a composite blends them into one new chart by taking the midpoint of each pair of positions.

docs.title: How Zodiac builds one
docs.text:
Zodiac synthesizes the composite from two source files — the two charts you want to combine. For each body it computes the midpoint of the two positions, and those midpointed positions become the planets of the composite chart. The house cusps are composite-derived, so the resulting chart is a self-consistent whole that can be read like any other chart in the program: drawn on the wheel, shown in the Tables view, and explored with harmonics and aspects.

Because a composite is a genuine chart in its own right, it can also be progressed. Zodiac carries progressed-composite handling, so you can advance the composite in symbolic time the same way you would a natal chart (see Progressions).

a composite chart wheel synthesized from two neutral demo charts, with the midpointed planetary positions and composite-derived house cusps

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Reach for a composite when you want the relationship itself as a single object of study — one wheel whose planets and houses describe the combined pair. When instead you want to see how two charts interact — which planets aspect which, transits against a birth chart, or a synastry comparison — use a bi-wheel, which keeps the two charts distinct and highlights the aspects between them.

docs.title: Progressions
docs.text: Secondary progressions advance a chart forward in symbolic time — the familiar "a day for a year" technique — so that the slow unfolding of a life can be read against the birth chart. Zodiac treats progressions the same way it treats every other kind of moving contact: as events that you find in a table rather than charts you cast by hand.

docs.title: Progressions as events
docs.text:
In the Events panel, progressions appear under the P=P category, and the engine reports them in two directions:

  • Progressed-to-natal — the progressed planets aspecting the positions they held at birth.
  • Progressed-to-progressions — aspects that form between the progressed planets themselves as they advance.

Enable progressions in the event-filter toolbar, give the panel a date range, and Zodiac lists the progressed contacts that fall inside it in the same dated, sorted table as your transits and returns. As with every event, clicking a row brings up the corresponding chart, so you can see the progressed aspect drawn in context — often as chart #2 in a bi-wheel against the natal chart.

Because progressions live in the shared events table, they can be filtered and combined with other event types on a per-tab basis, and you can narrow a search to specific bodies using the pattern search language — for example, restricting the list to the progressed contacts you care about rather than the full set.

the Events panel with the P=P filter enabled, showing a list of progressed-to-natal and progressed-to-progression events for a neutral demo chart

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: A return chart is cast for the moment a planet comes back to the exact position it held at birth. The most familiar is the solar return — the instant each year when the transiting Sun regains its natal longitude — but Zodiac also casts sidereal returns, so the technique works whichever zodiac you are studying in.

docs.title: Returns and the harmonic setting
docs.text: Return charts respect the program's current harmonic setting, which opens up a useful shortcut. Because a harmonic divides the circle into equal parts, asking for a return while a harmonic is active gives you the nearest sub-return. Enter H4 and request a return and Zodiac generates the nearest quarterly return — a quarter of the way around the Sun's cycle — which may of course be the full return itself. In the same way you can reach demi-returns and other fractional returns simply by choosing the harmonic first. See Harmonics on the wheel for how the harmonic display setting works elsewhere in the program.

docs.title: Finding returns through the Events panel
docs.text:
You do not have to know the date of a return to cast it. Enable returns in the event-filter toolbar, set a date range, and the Events panel lists every return that falls inside it, alongside a summary of the aspects in orb at that moment. Clicking a return row brings up the return chart — typically as chart #2 in a bi-wheel against the natal chart, so you can read the return against the radix at a glance. Returns sit in the same table as stations and ingresses, so a single search can gather all the key annual moments together.

the Events panel showing a solar return row selected, with the aspects-in-orb summary for that return, using a neutral demo chart

docs.title: Returns and primary-direction timing
docs.text: Return charts also feed the program's timing work: a solar return (including demi- and quarti-solar returns) is the basis for PSSR timing — the primary solar/sidereal-return method. That relationship is covered in Primary directions & quotidian modes.

docs.title: The Chart Wheel in Depth
docs.text:
The chart wheel is Zodiac's central view — the round diagram of signs, houses, planets, and aspects. It is more than a static picture, though. The wheel responds to a set of view-level choices — which zodiac you read the chart in, which house system and aspects you use, which harmonic you draw, and which coordinate frame you measure in — and it can show layers that most charting programs leave to separate tools: fixed stars, midpoint structures, a declination strip, and animated motion through time.

Because these are display settings rather than properties of the chart itself, changing them never alters the saved chart or forces a recalculation of the underlying data. You can move freely between a tropical and a sidereal reading, or redraw the same wheel in the fourth harmonic, without casting anything new.

the chart wheel filling the center of the window for a neutral demo chart, with the aspect-set and harmonic controls in the status bar

  • Harmonics on the wheel — redraw the wheel in any harmonic and show dynamic harmonic aspect lines from H1 to H32.
  • Fixed stars — the stars the wheel shows near planets, and why.
  • Midpoints — how midpoint structures are drawn on the wheel.

The related Harmonics tab lists and navigates the same harmonic and midpoint structures the wheel can draw.

docs.title: Animation, Scrubbing & Paran Cycling
docs.text:
The chart wheel doesn't have to hold a single moment. Zodiac can animate it through time — playing or stepping through the events you found in the Events panel and watching the planets move around the wheel as an aspect comes into orb, peaks, and separates.

the Aspect Range Navigator transport — play/stop and first/prev/peak/next/last controls — in the title bar of the Events panel

docs.title: The Aspect Range Navigator
docs.text:
Ranged aspect events — a transit that stays in orb over a span of days — are driven by the Aspect Range Navigator, which sits in the title bar of the Events panel, to the right of the panel name (it can be hidden in Settings → Events). Its transport lets you play and stop, and step through the significant moments of the range:

  • first / prev / peak / next / last — jump to the start of the range, back one step, the moment of closest aspect, forward one step, or the end.

As it plays, the planets slide around the wheel in smooth discrete steps, with the aspect lines crossfading and the glyphs tweening from one position to the next, so you see the configuration form and dissolve rather than jumping between frames. When cycling through paran events, the same first/prev/peak/next/last controls snap to the focal paran moments.

docs.title: Rotation lock
docs.text: During continuous playback, a rotation lock freezes the wheel's orientation. Without it, keeping a moving Ascendant on the left edge would spin the whole ring while the planets appeared to stay put. With the lock on, the ring holds still and the planets visibly sweep around it — which is usually what you want to watch.

docs.title: Scrub mode
docs.text: You can also drag the wheel through time directly. In scrub mode, dragging skips the expensive recomputation that would otherwise fire on every intermediate moment, so the drag stays responsive; when you release, Zodiac performs a single exact catch-up recompute at the position you landed on. Play, pause, and resume remember where you paused, so you can stop to examine a moment and pick up again from there.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: Animation is the visual companion to the event list — find the events in the Events panel, then play or scrub through them here. Paran cycling connects to Paranatellonta.

docs.title: Prime Vertical, Equatorial & Great-Circle Aspects
docs.text: By default, aspects are measured along the ecliptic — the familiar circle of the zodiac. But the ecliptic is only one way to slice the sky, and some questions are answered better in another frame. Zodiac lets you view and aspect a chart in coordinate frames beyond the ecliptic, and the aspect mode can be chosen independently of the other display settings.

docs.title: Prime vertical (PV / "mundoscope")
docs.text:
The prime vertical frame — sometimes called the mundoscope — redraws the chart around the local horizon and meridian rather than the zodiac. This is the frame to use when you want to know whether a body is really on the horizon or the meridian, as opposed to merely sharing a degree of ecliptic longitude with an angle. It is especially useful for inspecting parans, where what matters is exactly this angular placement; see Paranatellonta.

Rough edges

The prime-vertical wheel rendering has some known rough edges — the aspects are computed and displayed, but the drawn wheel is not yet perfectly correct in this mode. For bi-wheels, the PV display has been corrected so the two charts share a common reference frame, which makes it the better choice for visualizing paran coincidences between two charts.

docs.title: Equatorial aspects
docs.text: You can also aspect in the equatorial frame, measured along the celestial equator rather than the ecliptic. For equatorial transits, Zodiac uses an "ex-precession" technique, which accounts for precession when comparing moving equatorial positions against the natal chart.

docs.title: Great-circle mode
docs.text:
Great-circle mode measures aspects by the true great-circle distance between two bodies on the sphere — the shortest arc joining them — rather than by their difference in one coordinate. This is honored consistently across the program: both the chart wheel's aspect display and the event search use great-circle distances when this mode is on, so a search will find exactly the contacts the wheel draws.

the aspect-mode selector in the status bar (Ecliptic / Equatorial); the GC (great-circle) and Mundane toggles sit beside it

docs.title: The Declination Strip
docs.text:
Alongside the chart wheel, Zodiac can show a declination strip — a narrow panel that plots each body's declination (its angular distance north or south of the celestial equator) beside the others. Where the wheel shows longitude around a circle, the strip lays the planets out by declination so you can read their north–south spread at a glance.

the declination strip beside the chart wheel for a neutral demo chart, with planetary declination labels placed down the strip

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
The strip makes declination aspects easy to spot:

  • Parallels — two bodies at nearly the same declination on the same side of the equator (both north, or both south).
  • Contraparallels — two bodies at nearly the same declination on opposite sides.

These are the declination analogues of the conjunction and opposition, and they can be significant even when the bodies show no ordinary ecliptic aspect. Placing the declinations side by side makes matching values line up visually, so parallels and contraparallels stand out without arithmetic.

docs.title: Readable labels
docs.text: When several planets sit at similar declinations their labels would naturally collide. Zodiac uses multi-pass label placement to nudge the labels apart, reducing overlap so the strip stays readable even in a crowded region.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: For north–south angular relationships that involve the horizon and meridian rather than the equator — parallels of a different kind — see the declination display mode of the Speculum.

docs.title: Fixed Stars
docs.text:
The chart wheel shows fixed stars that fall close to a planet. Specifically, a star is drawn when it lies within about 1.5° direct distance of a planet — that is, the true great-circle separation between the two points measured in two dimensions, not just the difference in ecliptic longitude. A star that looks close by longitude but is well off in latitude will not qualify, and rightly so: it isn't really near the planet on the sphere.

a chart wheel where a fixed star is drawn beside a planet it conjoins within great-circle orb

docs.title: The philosophy behind it
docs.text:
Fixed stars are only shown when there is a real reason to consider them. The guiding idea is that if a fixed star matters to a chart, it does so in one of two ways:

  • It is genuinely close to a planet in great-circle terms — a tight conjunction on the sphere, which is what the ~1.5° direct-distance rule captures on the wheel; or
  • It is involved in a paran with a planet — an angular coincidence, where the star and a planet reach the horizon or meridian together, regardless of how far apart they are by longitude.

Keeping the wheel to stars that pass the first test avoids cluttering it with dozens of catalog stars that happen to share a degree of longitude but are nowhere near the planet on the sphere.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: The second kind of relevance — stars that matter because they share an angular moment with a planet — is not a wheel-conjunction question at all. It is handled through parans: see Paranatellonta and the Speculum. In the parans work, star-to-star parans are deliberately excluded and only the planet-to-star parans that carry astrological meaning are kept.

docs.title: The Harmonics Tab
docs.text:
The Harmonics tab is the list-and-navigate companion to the harmonic and midpoint structures the chart wheel can draw. Where the wheel shows the geometry, this tab shows a tree of every harmonic aspect and midpoint in the chart, and lets you click your way straight to any of them.

the Harmonics tab showing the tree of harmonic aspects and midpoints, with an overtone child expanded under a harmonic group

docs.title: Three ways to sort
docs.text:
The same list can be sorted three ways, depending on what you're hunting for:

  • By harmonic — grouped by number (all the H4 contacts, all the H9 contacts, and so on).
  • By planetary combination — grouped by the bodies involved, so you can see every harmonic relationship between, say, Sun and Saturn together.
  • By orb — tightest contacts first, so the strongest relationships rise to the top.

docs.title: Overtones
docs.text:
The tree includes overtones — a way of seeing one harmonic's pattern nested inside another. You can find the H4 patterns (squares) inside an H9 chart, or, the other way around, the H9 patterns (noviles) inside an H4 chart. Overtones appear as child entries beneath their parent harmonic.

The tab works for both single wheels and bi-wheels.

docs.title: Clicking through to the wheel
docs.text:
Clicking an entry drives the chart wheel directly:

  • Click a harmonic or midpoint entry to highlight it and redraw the chart's aspect lines to focus those aspects, and/or switch the wheel to that harmonic.
  • Ctrl-click a harmonic entry to switch the wheel to that harmonic and set the bodies involved as focal planets.
  • Click an overtone child to jump to its parent harmonic group and overlay that overtone's aspect set on the wheel for direct visual inspection.

You can copy a selected entry with Ctrl+C.

Tip

Clearing focal planets returns the wheel to H1 and resets any aspect-set override, so it's easy to get back to a clean radix view after exploring.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: Harmonics on the wheel covers the harmonic control and the dynamic H1–H32 aspect display that these clicks drive.

docs.title: Harmonics on the Wheel
docs.text: Harmonics are a way of looking at a chart through a single number. In the n-th harmonic, every position is multiplied by n and wrapped back into the circle, so that planets which form an n-th-harmonic aspect in the natal chart — for example squares in the fourth harmonic, or noviles in the ninth — line up as conjunctions. Zodiac lets you explore this directly on the wheel, without casting a separate harmonic chart.

docs.title: The harmonic control
docs.text:
A harmonic control on the wheel lets you type a number and redraw the current chart in that harmonic. The default is H1 — the ordinary radix chart. Enter 4 and the same wheel is redrawn in the fourth harmonic; return it to 1 for the natal view. Because the harmonic is a view-level display setting, this switch is instant and never creates a new chart file.

the chart wheel redrawn in the 5th harmonic, with the harmonic selector at the right of the status bar set to 5

docs.title: Dynamic harmonic aspect lines (H1–H32)
docs.text:
Rather than redrawing the whole wheel, you can also overlay harmonic aspect lines from H1 all the way to H32 on the ordinary chart. Each harmonic is toggled individually from a row of buttons on the status bar, which appears when the Harmonic aspect set is selected — click a harmonic's button to add its aspect lines, click again to remove them. This makes it easy to build up exactly the set of harmonics you want to see.

For example, the classical Ptolemaic aspects correspond to the harmonic set 1 2 3 6 8 (conjunction, opposition, trine, sextile, and semi-square/sesquiquadrate), so enabling just those buttons gives a traditional aspect picture.

As with ordinary aspects, aspect intensity is shown by line thickness — the closer the aspect, the heavier the line — so the strongest harmonic contacts stand out even when several harmonics are displayed together.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: For a sortable, navigable list of every harmonic and midpoint structure in the chart — including "overtones," which let you see one harmonic's pattern inside another — use the Harmonics tab. Clicking an entry there can redraw the wheel's aspect lines or switch the wheel to that harmonic for you.

docs.title: House Systems & Aspects
docs.text: Two of the choices that most shape how a chart reads are the house system — how the sky is divided into the twelve houses — and the aspects you count between bodies. Zodiac lets you set both, and treats them as view-level display options: changing them redraws the current chart without recasting it or marking the file as modified.

docs.title: House systems
docs.text:
Zodiac supports nine house systems, so you can draw the same chart under whichever division your practice uses and compare cusps side by side. Because the house system is a display setting, switching it simply redraws the wheel's cusps.

In some displays the houses are labeled with house glyphs rather than plain numbers, which keeps a busy wheel readable and matches the glyph styling used elsewhere in the program.

the control listing the nine available house systems, with one selected

docs.title: Aspects
docs.text:
Zodiac ships with a large aspect library — over forty aspects — reaching well beyond the familiar conjunction, sextile, square, trine, and opposition into the minor and harmonic aspects. You rarely want all of them drawn at once, so two controls keep the wheel legible:

  • Aspect-set selection. Choose which set of aspects is active — for example a classical Ptolemaic set, or a wider set that includes minor aspects — so only the aspects you care about are calculated and drawn.
  • Adjustable orbs. Set how wide the allowance is for an aspect to count. Tighter orbs show only the closest contacts; wider orbs surface more, at the cost of a busier wheel.

The strength of each aspect that is drawn is shown by the thickness of its line — a tighter, stronger aspect draws a heavier line than a loose one — so you can read the important contacts at a glance. This intensity styling is shared with the harmonic aspect display; see Harmonics on the wheel.

Harmonic aspects are handled separately

The forty-plus aspects here are the classic geometric ones. If you think of aspects as harmonics — squares as the fourth harmonic, noviles as the ninth, and so on — the dynamic H1–H32 display on Harmonics on the wheel and the Harmonics tab is the more direct way to work.

docs.title: Midpoints
docs.text:
A midpoint is the point exactly halfway between two planets, and midpoint work asks which third body sits on that halfway point. Written in the usual shorthand, a midpoint structure is A = B/C: planet A is at the midpoint of B and C. Zodiac can draw these structures directly on the chart wheel, so you can see the geometry rather than reading it off a table.

a chart wheel showing a midpoint structure — a dashed chord between two planets with a solid line running to the focal planet on the midpoint

docs.title: How midpoints are drawn
docs.text:
• The B/C pair is shown as a dashed chord line drawn directly between the two constituent planets.
  • The focal planet A is joined to that structure by an orb-weighted solid line — the closer A sits to the exact midpoint, the heavier the line — so tight midpoint contacts stand out from loose ones at a glance.

docs.title: Midpoint-to-midpoint patterns
docs.text: Zodiac also draws the more elaborate A/B = C/D case, where two different midpoint pairs fall on the same axis. When two midpoint pairs share an axis like this, the wheel connects them, again with orb-weighted line thickness, so these longer midpoint chains are visible as a single structure.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: Midpoints are closely related to harmonics — both are ways of finding hidden geometric relationships in a chart — and the Harmonics tab lists a chart's midpoints alongside its harmonic aspects, sortable and clickable. To search for the moment a midpoint is triggered over a date range (for example Ura/Plu=Nep), use the event engine's pattern search.

docs.title: Zodiacs & Ayanamshas
docs.text: Zodiac can draw a chart in either the tropical or a sidereal zodiac. The two differ in where they place 0° Aries. The tropical zodiac ties 0° Aries to the vernal equinox — the Sun's position at the start of spring — so the signs stay locked to the seasons. A sidereal zodiac instead ties the signs to the stars, and because the equinox slowly drifts against the stars (precession), a sidereal chart's degrees are offset from the tropical ones by an amount called the ayanamsha.

docs.title: The sidereal options
docs.text:
Zodiac offers three sidereal schemes:

  • The original "constellational" sidereal (listed as Sidereal in the zodiac selector) — inherited from the base program. This is a non-equal, 13-sign scheme meant to follow the actual constellations, which vary in width and can include Ophiuchus where the ecliptic crosses it. Some astrologers prefer this literal, star-boundary approach.
  • Fagan–Bradley — an equal-sign, 30°-per-sign ayanamsha that fixes the star Aldebaran at 15° Taurus. It is the standard among Western sidereal practitioners.
  • Lahiri — an equal-sign, 30°-per-sign ayanamsha that fixes Spica at 0° Libra. It is the common choice in Jyotish (Vedic) astrology.

The two equal-sign ayanamshas were added to the sidereal branch specifically for western-sidereal and Vedic work; there is good evidence the Babylonians used equal-portioned 30° signs, not just constellation boundaries.

Apparent, not true, positions

Aspects are computed from apparent positions rather than true positions. Most commercial astrology software uses apparent positions, so this keeps Zodiac's results consistent with the tools you may be comparing against.

docs.title: Switching zodiac
docs.text:
The zodiac is a view-level setting: it controls how the current chart is displayed and is not saved into the chart file. Changing it redraws the wheel without recasting the chart, so you can compare a tropical and a sidereal reading of the same data freely. The house system, aspect set, harmonic, and coordinate frame behave the same way — see House systems & aspects.

the zodiac selector in the status bar, open to show Tropical, Sidereal, Fagan-Bradley and Lahiri

docs.title: Events (Transits)
docs.text:
The Events panel is where Zodiac looks through time. Instead of a single moment, it searches a range of dates and lists the astrological events that fall inside it — transits, progressions, stations, ingresses, returns, parans, and heliacal apparitions — with the timing worked out for you. It is the most actively developed part of the program, and the goal for it is simple: make finding events quick, easy, and powerful.

the Events panel down the right side of the window, with the filter toolbar at the top, a date range, and the scrolling list of dated events

docs.title: What it finds
docs.text:
For a given chart and date range, the engine can report:

  • Transits to transits (T=T) — aspects between the moving planets themselves.
  • Transits to natal (T=N) — the moving planets aspecting the birth chart.
  • Progressions (P=P) — secondary progressions, to natal and to progressions.
  • Stations — where a planet turns retrograde or direct, including the surrounding shadow period.
  • Ingresses — a planet entering a new sign.
  • Returns — solar, sidereal, and (with a harmonic set) quarterly or demi-returns.
  • Parans — planet-to-planet and planet-to-star angular coincidences (see Parans & Primary Directions).
  • Heliacal apparitions — a body's arc of visibility, from morning-first rising to evening-last setting (see Heliacal apparitions).

Which of these appear is controlled by the event-filter toolbar at the top of the panel, and every setting is remembered per tab, so two charts open side by side can be searching for entirely different things.

docs.title: Two ways to search
docs.text:
Browse everything in range. Leave the filters wide and Zodiac lists all the events of the enabled types across your date span. This is fast: on an optimized build, about a second for a year of transits-to-transits, transits-to-natal, returns, and stations — and roughly four seconds if you sweep every harmonic from H1 through H32.

Search for something specific. Type a pattern into the search field and Zodiac finds just those events. The pattern language is compact but expressive — a few examples:

You type You get Sun=Moon Every lunation (Sun conjunct Moon) in range H4 Mars=Saturn Fourth-harmonic (square) contacts of Mars and Saturn Mars ingress Aries Mars entering Aries Saturn station Saturn's stations Ura/Plu=Sun-r The Uranus/Pluto midpoint contacting radix (natal) Sun Sun,Moon,Mars Three-body clusters of Sun, Moon, and Mars

The full language — group tokens, harmonic prefixes, midpoints, exact multi-body patterns, and the transit/natal/progressed suffixes — is covered in The pattern search language.

docs.title: Working with the results
docs.text:
• Click an event to load that moment on the chart wheel, so you can see the aspect in context.
  • Relocate it. An event is normally tied to the chart's location, but you can edit a single event — locking its time zone — to cast it for somewhere else. See Relocating an event.
  • Step or play through a range. Ranged events (a transit that is in orb over a span of days) can be animated with the Aspect Range Navigator — play, stop, and step first / previous / peak / next / last — while the wheel animates the planets across it. See Animation, scrubbing & paran cycling.
  • Skip the noise. Each tab can skip events shorter than a chosen duration and auto-refresh on demand.

docs.title: Long searches don't freeze the program
docs.text:
Pattern searches can run in the background. A long search can keep going when you switch to another tab, and paused or backgrounded finders reconnect and repopulate their results when you return. See Background finders & performance for the controls and the settings that govern them.

Next: The event-filter toolbar  ·  The pattern search language  ·  Heliacal apparitions

docs.title: Heliacal Apparitions
docs.text:
A heliacal event is about a body's visibility against the Sun — when it first rises before dawn, when it is last seen after dusk, and the phases in between. Zodiac treats these not as scattered points but as a single, navigable apparition, so you can step through a body's whole season of visibility from one event. Turn them on with the Heliacal toggle on the event-filter toolbar.

a heliacal apparition event selected in the Events list, with the Aspect Range Navigator showing its five labeled stops (MF, Acr, Cul, Cs, EL) for a neutral demo chart

docs.title: One apparition, not many points
docs.text:
For fixed stars and the outer planets (Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn), Zodiac reports a single apparition: the arc of visibility running from the body's morning-first rising (MF) to its evening-last setting (EL). Rather than listing loose phase points, it anchors the whole apparition at the body's culmination (Cul) — its midnight meridian transit, which falls near opposition, when the body is highest and best seen.

The Aspect Range Navigator steps through five labeled stops along the arc:

MF · acronychal rising (Acr) · culmination (Cul) · cosmical setting (Cs) · EL

docs.title: A nuance worth understanding
docs.text:
Acr and Cs are visibility phases in the sense of Ptolemy's Phaseis, not ordinary rise/set times:

  • Acronychal rising (Acr) is the date the body rises exactly at sunset.
  • Cosmical setting (Cs) is the date the body sets exactly at sunrise.

Crucially, these are not the rise and set of the culmination night. Each is computed for the date on which that exact dusk or dawn coincidence actually occurs, so Acr and Cs fall on their own dates — dates that can lie weeks away from the culmination, and can even appear in a counter-intuitive order around it. This is expected: they mark genuine astronomical phases, not events of a single evening.

docs.title: Other bodies
docs.text:
The apparition model fits the slow outer bodies. The faster ones are handled differently:

  • Inner planets (Mercury and Venus) give two greatest-elongation apparitions per synodic cycle — one as a morning star, one as an evening star — rather than a single MF-to-EL arc.
  • The Moon keeps its discrete crescent events, listed as individual occurrences.

In every case the events use the same discrete-occurrence transport as parans, so you can step between them the same way you cycle paran moments.

Next: Relocating an event  ·  Background finders & performance

docs.title: The Pattern Search Language
docs.text:
The event-filter toolbar is good at browsing everything in range. When you want a particular event — the moment two specific planets square each other, a midpoint contact, an ingress — you type a pattern into the Events search field and Zodiac finds just those events. The language is compact but expressive, and it is the quickest way to ask the engine a precise question.

the Events search field with a pattern typed in and a green (valid) border, the most-recently-used dropdown open beneath it, and matching dated events in the list below

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text:
At its simplest a pattern names two bodies joined by =, which means "in aspect": Sun=Moon finds every lunation (Sun conjunct Moon) in range. From there the language adds patterns of three or more bodies, harmonics, ingresses, stations, midpoints, role suffixes, and group tokens. Multiple patterns can be run at once by separating them with a semicolon (;).

You type You get Sun=Moon A pairwise aspect: every Sun–Moon contact in range Sun=Moon=Mars An exact pattern: all three bodies in orb simultaneously Sun,Moon,Mars A flexible cluster: any pairwise aspects among the three H4 Mars=Saturn Fourth-harmonic (square) contacts of Mars and Saturn Mars ingress Aries Mars entering the sign Aries Saturn station Saturn's stations (retrograde or direct turns) Ura/Plu=Nep The Uranus/Pluto midpoint contacting Neptune Ura/Plu=Sun-r The Uranus/Pluto midpoint contacting radix (natal) Sun OT=Venus Any outer planet aspecting Venus Sun=Moon; Mars ingress Aries Two searches at once, separated by ;

docs.title: Exact patterns vs. clusters
docs.text: The distinction between = and , matters. An equals-delimited pattern of three or more bodies (Sun=Moon=Mars) registers as an exact pattern: the finder reports only the windows where every body is within orb at the same time, and searches for the moment the configuration is tightest. A comma-delimited list (Sun,Moon,Mars) instead generates flexible pairwise detection — any aspect among the members counts, so the three need not all line up together.

docs.title: Harmonics
docs.text: Prefix a pattern with a harmonic to change which aspect it looks for: H4 Mars=Saturn seeks the fourth-harmonic (square) contact. The prefix accepts richer specifiers as well — divisor expansion and capped or dedicated harmonic sets — so a single pattern can be tied to exactly the harmonics you want.

docs.title: Midpoints
docs.text: Write a midpoint with a slash: Ura/Plu is the Uranus/Pluto midpoint. A midpoint can sit on either side of the =, as in Ura/Plu=Nep (a topical search over recent years) or Ura/Plu=Sun-r. Patterns that contain a midpoint use a tighter effective orb.

docs.title: Role suffixes
docs.text:
Append a suffix to fix a body's role in the search:

  • -t — transiting (the moving body)
  • -r — radix, i.e. natal
  • -p — progressed

So Ura/Plu=Sun-r pins the Sun to the natal chart while the midpoint transits.

docs.title: Group tokens
docs.text:
A group token stands for a whole list of bodies and auto-expands when the search runs:

  • OT — the outer planets
  • IP — the inner planets
  • N — natal bodies
  • T — transiting bodies
  • P — progressed bodies
  • NA — the natal angles

OT=N therefore expands to every outer planet against every natal body. Multi-member sides are distributed into the individual exact patterns they imply.

docs.title: Feedback and recall
docs.text:
The search field validates as you type: a green border means the pattern parses, a red border means it does not. The field is backed by a most-recently-used list with substring completion, so a pattern you have run before is a keystroke away. Long searches show a progress cue — a gradient that sweeps the field — while they run, and can continue in the background (see Background finders & performance).

Next: Stations, ingresses & returns  ·  Heliacal apparitions

docs.title: Background Finders & Performance
docs.text: The event engine is built to stay quick even when you ask a lot of it, and to keep working without freezing the rest of the program. This page covers how fast the common searches are, what happens during a long one, and the settings that govern background work.

docs.title: How fast it is
docs.text: The Events panel is designed for speed. On an optimized build, a full year of the common event types — transits-to-transits, transits-to-natal, returns-to-natal, and stations — takes about a second. Sweeping every harmonic from H1 through H32 over the same range takes roughly four seconds. Most of the time you will not notice the search running at all; a few kinds of search, such as aspect-pattern matching, are naturally heavier because the engine has to find each configuration's in-orb window and its moment of closest orb.

docs.title: Searches that run in the background
docs.text:
Long pattern searches do not have to hold you at one tab. With the optional backgroundFinders setting enabled, a search can continue running when you switch to another tab, so you can keep working while the engine grinds through a wide range or a demanding pattern. Each finder tracks its own state and can be paused, resumed, or canceled per tab.

When you come back, paused or backgrounded finders reconnect and repopulate their results — the list you left behind fills in as the finder catches up, rather than starting over. A long-running search also shows a progress cue in the search field so you can see it is still working.

Note

backgroundFinders is a persisted preference. Leave it off and searches run in the foreground for the active tab; turn it on when you routinely launch long searches and want to keep moving between tabs.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Zodiac caches results and validates the cache carefully, so switching tabs or re-opening the same chart does not trigger a needless recomputation. View-only changes — harmonic, house system, zodiac, aspect set — are treated as display settings and do not by themselves force the events to be found again. The upshot is that the program does the expensive work once and reuses it whenever the inputs have not actually changed.

Back to: Events (Transits)  ·  The pattern search language

docs.title: Relocating an Event
docs.text:
The events in a search are all cast for the chart's location — the place tied to the tab you are working in. Sometimes, though, you want to see how a single event would look somewhere else: what was on the horizon at a different city when a transit came exact, or how a return chart falls if you were away from home. Zodiac lets you relocate one event without disturbing the rest of the list.

an event's detail editor open, with the time-zone field locked and a new location entered, ready to produce a relocated event chart

docs.title: How to relocate
docs.text:
1. Click the event in the Events list to select it.
  2. Edit its details — open the event's editor and change the location to the place you want.
  3. Lock the time zone so that relocating the event holds its moment in time while moving the observer, rather than reinterpreting the clock time at the new place.

Zodiac then produces an individually relocated event chart for that single event. The rest of the search stays put, tied to the original location, so relocating one event is a one-off inspection rather than a change to the whole tab.

Tip

This is a quick way to compare an event across places — cast it at home, relocate a copy elsewhere, and read the two side by side in a bi-wheel.

Next: Background finders & performance

docs.title: Stations, Ingresses & Returns
docs.text:
Alongside aspects, the Events panel reports three kinds of event that are about a single body's own motion or timing: stations, ingresses, and returns. Each has a filter on the event-filter toolbar, and each can also be searched for by pattern.

the Events list showing a station row with its shadow-period entry and exit dates, an ingress row, and a return row, for a neutral demo chart

docs.title: Stations
docs.text: A planet stations when it appears to stop and reverse direction — turning retrograde, or turning direct again. Zodiac lists these turning points and, around each one, demarcates the shadow period: the span over which the planet travels back and forth across the same stretch of zodiac. The entrance and exit of the shadow are found by searching for the transit of the station degree, so the whole retrograde episode — not just the instant of the turn — is laid out for you. Search for them by pattern with, for example, Saturn station.

docs.title: Ingresses
docs.text: An ingress is a body crossing a boundary into a new division of the chart. Zodiac tracks both sign ingresses (a planet entering the next zodiac sign) and house ingresses (a planet crossing a house cusp). Sign index resolution is handled correctly for forward and reverse (retrograde) crossings, so a planet that ingresses, retrogrades back, and re-enters is reported faithfully. Search by pattern with Mars ingress Aries.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
A return is the moment a body comes back to its natal position. Zodiac finds solar and sidereal returns, and — because returns integrate with the current harmonic setting — a harmonic set turns them into quarterly or demi-returns. Enter a harmonic (for instance H4) and select a return, and Zodiac generates the nearest quarterly return, which may be the actual return. Each return event also carries a summary of the aspects in orb at that moment, so you can read its flavor at a glance before opening the chart.

Tip

Because returns follow the harmonic setting, you never have to cast a demi- or quarti-return by hand — set the harmonic, pick the return, and the event engine finds the moment for you.

For the return charts themselves — how they are constructed and displayed — see Returns.

Next: Heliacal apparitions  ·  Relocating an event

docs.title: The Event-Filter Toolbar
docs.text:
Every Events panel carries a small toolbar across the top that decides which kinds of events the finder looks for. Rather than casting new charts or digging through a settings dialog, you flip the event types you care about on and off right here, and the list below refreshes to match. Everything on this toolbar is remembered per tab and saved with the session, so two charts open side by side can be hunting for completely different things.

the event-filter toolbar at the top of the Events panel: the S (stations) and R (returns) buttons, then the T, P, AP, PD, Par and Hel groups, whose dropdowns hold the individual event types (T=T, T=N, P=P and so on), with the skip-by-duration and refresh buttons at the left

docs.title: The three core toggles
docs.text:
The heart of the toolbar is a row of type toggles:

  • T=T — transiting to transiting: aspects between the moving planets themselves.
  • T=N — transiting to natal: the moving planets aspecting the birth chart.
  • P=P — progressed to progressed: secondary progressions to progressions (and to natal).

Turn on as many as you like. With all three lit, the list mixes every kind of contact in range; narrow it to just T=N, say, when you only want to watch transits landing on the natal chart.

docs.title: Sub-mode groups
docs.text:
Alongside the core toggles are split-button groups that gather related event types under a single control with a dropdown. As of v0.9.9 these grouped controls replace the older row of individual filter actions, keeping the toolbar compact. They include:

  • Ingresses — a planet entering a new sign (or house). See Stations, ingresses & returns.
  • Paranatellonta (parans) — planet-to-planet and planet-to-star angular coincidences. See Parans & Primary Directions.
  • Heliacal — a toggle that adds heliacal apparitions to the search. See Heliacal apparitions.

Stations and returns are likewise available as filters; open a group's dropdown to pick exactly which sub-modes it contributes.

docs.title: Trimming the results
docs.text:
Two more per-tab controls help keep the list readable:

  • Skip events shorter than a duration. A brief, fleeting contact can be filtered out by setting a minimum duration, so the list shows only events that stay in orb long enough to matter to you.
  • Auto-refresh. Each tab can recompute its events on demand — or automatically — when you change the range or the filters, so the list never falls out of step with the toolbar above it.

Tip

Because these settings live with the tab and travel in your session, a tab you have tuned for, say, outer-planet transits to natal will come back exactly that way the next time you open your work.

Next: The pattern search language  ·  Background finders & performance

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This section takes you from a fresh download to a chart on the screen. If you have never opened Zodiac before, work through the pages in order; if you are returning, jump to whichever step you need.

The program is compact and dock-based, and its use model is chart- and table-based rather than menu-driven. Once it is installed and you have cast a chart, most of the rest of this guide is about the many ways Zodiac lets you look at that chart and search through time around it.

  • Installing Zodiac — the Windows installer, what it packages, and a note for developers building from source.
  • A tour of the main window — the database tree, the toolbar, the central tabs, the Events panel, and the status bar.
  • Creating & editing charts — casting a chart, the file editor, and the chart file types.
  • Locations, time & calendars — place lookup, time modes, and historical-date handling.

docs.title: Creating & Editing Charts
docs.text:
To cast a chart in Zodiac you enter three things — a date, a time, and a place — and the program draws the wheel. You do this in the file editor, which you reach with the New button (for a fresh chart) or the Edit button (to change one you already have). See A tour of the main window for where those buttons are.

the chart file editor, showing the name field and chart type, the local date, time and time-zone controls, the location field, and the comment box

docs.title: The file editor
docs.text: The editor holds all the data that defines a chart: its name, its date and time, and its location. Place lookup, time modes (Zone Time, LMT, LAT), and calendar handling all live here too — those are covered in detail in Locations, time & calendars.

docs.title: Entering the date and time
docs.text: Date and time are entered with the AstroDateTimeEdit control, a field built for astrological work rather than everyday calendars. It handles the awkward cases robustly: BC years and calendar suffixes are entered directly, so historical charts cast correctly instead of tripping over the limits of an ordinary date picker.

docs.title: Chart file types
docs.text: Every chart has a type. The most common is a plain natal chart, but Zodiac also stores a range of derived chart types — returns, progressions, composites, and others — plus an "Other" catch-all. Choose the type from the file-type dropdown in the editor. For what each type means and how to work with it, see Chart Types.

docs.title: The basis chart
docs.text: A derived chart is derived from something — a return is a return to a natal chart, a progression progresses one. When you pick a derived type, the editor offers a basis-chart selector so you can point the new chart at the chart it is based on. The selector looks through your database, including subfolders, to find candidate charts.

docs.title: Saving and loading
docs.text: Save the current chart with Save Chart; use Save As when you want to keep the original and write a copy under a new name. Loading is resilient to legacy formats — older chart files, including ones saved by earlier versions, open without fuss — so your existing collection carries forward.

docs.title: Installing Zodiac
docs.text:
Zodiac ships as a single Windows installer, built with the Nullsoft Scriptable Install System (NSIS). Download the latest version, run the installer, and follow the prompts.

the Zodiac NSIS installer, showing the install-location page and, if reached, the optional Google Maps API key prompt

docs.title: What the installer sets up
docs.text:
The installer is self-contained — it packages everything the program needs to run, so there is nothing else to download:

  • the required Qt runtime libraries (DLLs);
  • the application's resources — images, styles, and interpretation text;
  • the fonts Zodiac renders its glyphs and tables with — Almagest (the astrological glyph font) and the DejaVu family (DejaVu Sans, DejaVu Sans Condensed, and DejaVu Serif) — which it installs into the Windows Fonts directory and registers so the glyphs display correctly; and
  • the Swiss Ephemeris data files used for all astronomical calculations.

During installation you may also be offered an optional Google Maps API key field. This key enables online place and time-zone lookup; you can enter it now or add it later. See Locations, time & calendars for what the key is for and how to supply one afterward.

docs.title: Where your files live
docs.text:
Zodiac keeps your work and your settings out of the install directory so they are easy to back up or sync to the cloud:

  • Sessions and settings are stored under Documents/zodiac-charts.
  • The Google Maps API key is kept separately in APIKey.ini in the installation directory — it is deliberately not written into your settings file.

docs.title: Building on Linux
docs.text: Zodiac also builds and runs on Linux from source. You will need Qt 6.10.x or 6.11.x, the Boost C++ libraries, CMake, and a C++17 compiler. This is a developer path rather than a packaged download; for the full build steps and the current requirements, see the repository README.

docs.title: Locations, Time & Calendars
docs.text:
Casting an accurate chart means pinning down where and when precisely — the right latitude and longitude, the right time zone, and the right calendar for the era. Zodiac handles all three in the file editor.

the location and time controls in the file editor — the place-lookup field with a result selected, and the calendar-type and time-mode selectors

docs.title: Finding a location
docs.text:
Type a place name and Zodiac looks it up. There are two paths to a result:

  • Online lookup uses Google services to resolve a place to its latitude and longitude and to determine its time zone. This requires a Google Maps API key that you supply — either during installation, or by placing it in APIKey.ini in the install directory. See Installing Zodiac for where that file lives.
  • Offline lookup uses a bundled GeoNames city database (it prefers the cities500 dataset when present). This built-in database is used for transit time-zone resolution and for paran-latitude lookups, and it also serves as a fallback when online lookup is unavailable. In fact transit time zones now resolve from the local database first, only falling back online when the local zone can't be found.

When no API key is set, place lookup starts on the offline database; with a key it starts on Google. You can switch between them with the button beside the place field.

The offline database is what powers place-based paran work — see Paran latitude bands & city lookup.

docs.title: Time modes
docs.text:
Once the place is set, choose how the clock time should be interpreted:

  • Zone Time — ordinary civil (time-zone) time, the usual choice for modern charts.
  • LMT — local mean time, the mean-sun clock time for the exact longitude.
  • LAT — local apparent time, sundial time, which differs from mean time by the equation of time.

Zodiac applies the equation of time when converting between these modes, so LMT and LAT values round-trip exactly. This matters most for historical charts, where civil time zones did not yet exist.

docs.title: Calendars
docs.text:
The calendar type can be set to Auto, Gregorian, or Julian. Auto picks the calendar in civil use at the chart's date, which is the safe default; the explicit settings let you override it when you need to. Together with the time modes and the equation-of-time handling, this keeps historical dates correct — the reform from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar is accounted for rather than silently ignored.

Tip

For a modern birth chart you rarely need to change anything here: leave the calendar on Auto and the time on Zone Time. Reach for the other options when you are casting a chart from before the calendar reform, or working from a source that gives LMT or apparent time.

docs.title: A Tour of the Main Window
docs.text:
Zodiac's window is compact and dock-based: a set of panels arranged around a central chart area. The panels can be moved, floated, or hidden, so you can arrange the interface to suit the work you are doing. What follows describes the default layout.

the whole main window — the database tree on the left, the toolbar of icon buttons across the top, the tabbed chart area in the center, the Events panel docked on the right, and the status bar along the bottom

docs.title: The database tree (left)
docs.text: Down the left edge is the chart database — a tree of your saved charts and sessions, organized into folders you create. Open a chart from here and it appears in the central area. Sessions live in the same tree. See The chart database and Sessions & multi-window for organizing your work.

docs.title: The toolbar (top)
docs.text:
A row of icon buttons runs across the top of the window. From left to right, they let you:

  • New — start a new chart.
  • Edit — open the file editor for the current chart.
  • Save Chart — save the current chart to the database.
  • Save Session — save the current set of open tabs as a session.
  • Restore Session — reload a previously saved session.
  • Chart, Planets, Tables — switch the central area between the chart wheel, the planets view, and the text tables. See The Views.
  • Panels — show or hide the docked panels (Database, Details, Harmonics, Events, Speculum).
  • Settings — open the settings editor (zodiac, houses, aspects, orbs, and more). See Settings reference.
  • About — program information and credits.
  • Help — open this help. F1 opens the page for whatever is under focus or the mouse.

When the window is too narrow for every button, the last ones move into the toolbar's » overflow menu at its right-hand end.

a close-up of the toolbar across the top of the window, with the New, Edit, Save Chart, Save Session, Restore Session, Chart, Planets, Tables, Panels and Settings buttons

docs.title: The chart area (center)
docs.text: The central area is tabbed — each open chart or bi-wheel gets its own tab — and it shows the current chart in whichever view you have chosen: the chart wheel, the planets view, or the text tables.

docs.title: The Events panel (right)
docs.text: Docked on the right is the Events panel, where Zodiac searches a date range for transits, progressions, stations, ingresses, returns, parans, and heliacal apparitions. It is the most actively developed part of the program — see Events (Transits).

docs.title: The status bar (bottom)
docs.text:
Along the bottom is a status bar with the zodiac, house-system, aspect-set, aspect-mode and harmonic controls. When the aspect set is Harmonic, it also carries the dynamic-harmonic buttons, H1 through H32. Click a button to add or remove that harmonic's aspect lines on the chart wheel, so you can build up exactly the set you want to see — the Ptolemaic aspects, for example, are H1, H2, H3, H6, and H8. See Harmonics on the wheel.

the status bar along the bottom of the window with the Harmonic aspect set selected, showing the row of H1–H32 harmonic toggle buttons with several of them active

docs.title: Organizing Your Work
docs.text:
Once you have more than a handful of charts, two features keep everything tidy: the chart database and sessions. Together they mean you never have to hunt for a chart or rebuild your workspace by hand.

  • The Chart Database — a folder tree for your chart files. Group charts into folders and subfolders, move and copy them around, and reach the ones you used most recently. Because the files live in your Documents folder, they travel with any cloud-storage service you already use.

  • Sessions & Multi-Window — Zodiac remembers the tabs, views, and layout you had open and restores them next time. You can name a session to keep a line of research separate, and run more than one session at once.

docs.title: The Chart Database
docs.text:
The chart database is the panel that lists your saved charts as a folder tree. It is not a hidden, proprietary store — it is simply a view onto ordinary files in your Documents folder (typically Documents/zodiac-charts), so the way you organize charts here is the way they are organized on disk.

the chart database panel down the left side of the window, showing a folder tree with a couple of subfolders expanded and several demo charts inside them

docs.title: Folders and subfolders
docs.text: You can group related charts into folders, and folders within folders — for example a folder for family charts, another for mundane charts, or a folder per research project with dated subfolders inside it. Create a folder from the database panel, give it a name, and drag charts into it. There is no fixed depth, so you can nest subfolders as far as your organizing scheme needs.

docs.title: Moving and copying charts
docs.text: Charts can be moved from one folder to another, or copied so the same chart lives in more than one place. The quickest way is drag-and-drop: pick up a chart in the tree and drop it onto the folder where you want it. This makes reorganizing a large collection fast — rearrange the tree until it matches how you actually think about your charts.

docs.title: Recent charts
docs.text: The charts you have opened most recently are kept close at hand, so returning to something you were just working on does not mean digging back through the tree.

docs.title: Keeping charts everywhere: cloud storage
docs.text:
Because your charts are real files in your Documents folder, you can point any cloud-storage service — OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud Drive, and the like — at that folder and have your whole collection sync automatically. Open Zodiac on another machine that syncs the same folder and your charts are already there, arranged in the same tree.

Tip

The same is true for backups. Copying the zodiac-charts folder is enough to back up every chart, and your sessions live in the same user area, so they are backed up alongside them.

docs.title: Sessions & Multi-Window
docs.text:
A session is the whole state of your workspace: every open chart, its tabs, the view each one is showing, the transit date ranges you set, and the dock layout you arranged. Zodiac saves this automatically and restores it the next time you launch, so you can close the program mid-thought and pick up exactly where you left off.

the session list in the database panel, showing one named session and a couple of timestamped auto sessions, with the right-click context menu open

docs.title: Auto sessions vs. named sessions
docs.text:
By default your work is kept in a timestamped auto session — a file the program writes for you as you go, so nothing is lost between runs. When a piece of work is worth keeping separate, use Save Session As to promote the current session and give it a name. From then on the session has a tidy name of your choosing, your automatic saves update that named session, and the name appears in the title bar (for example, Zodiac – My Research Session), so you always know which workspace you are in.

Session files use the .zos extension (Zodiac Session) and are stored in your user documents area, alongside your charts — so they sync and back up the same way. Double-clicking a .zos file opens it in Zodiac.

docs.title: Managing sessions from the database
docs.text:
Sessions appear in the database panel. Right-click one for the actions you need:

  • Open in New Window — launch that session in a separate instance, so you can compare two workspaces side by side.
  • Load in Current — import the charts from a saved session into the workspace you already have open.
  • Rename — give a timestamped session a proper name, or change an existing one.
  • Delete — remove a session file you no longer need.

docs.title: One window, or several
docs.text: Zodiac runs as a single instance by default: if it is already open and you launch it again, the existing window is simply raised to the front rather than a second copy starting. When you genuinely want more than one workspace at once, you can start additional instances using command-line flags — --new for a fresh session, or --load-session to open a specific one. See Command-Line Options for the full list.

docs.title: Parans & Primary Directions
docs.text:
This section covers one of Zodiac's most distinctive corners: paranatellonta (parans for short) and the primary-direction timing bound up with them. If you have used other astrology software, be aware that Zodiac treats these techniques in a deliberately particular way — the design choices below are what make the feature its own.

the dedicated paran chart with the Speculum dock beside it, one paran highlighted, for a neutral demo chart

docs.title: What a paran is
docs.text:
A paran is an angular coincidence between two bodies. When one body is on an angle — rising, culminating, setting, or anti-culminating (at the lower meridian) — and, at that same instant and place, a second body is also on an angle, the two are said to be in paran. The bodies need not share the same angle: a planet rising while a star culminates is as much a paran as two planets rising together. Because the coincidence depends on the diurnal (daily) turning of the sky at a specific latitude, parans are a fundamentally mundane phenomenon rather than a zodiacal one — they live in the sky's rotation, not in ecliptic longitude.

Zodiac finds two kinds of paran participant: planet-to-planet and planet-to-star. The fixed stars come from a curated default selection.

docs.title: Why Zodiac's treatment is distinctive
docs.text:
Our implementation makes several opinionated choices, and it helps to know them up front:

  • Parans carry an effective date. Rather than presenting parans as timeless facts, Zodiac groups them with primary-direction timing so that each paran gets an effective date — roughly, when the angle acting as significator "meets" the other body by direction. This ties a static angular relationship to a moment in a life.
  • Star-to-star parans are excluded. Only planet-to-star (and planet-to-planet) parans are kept. Two fixed stars in paran with each other are not reported, on the view that a star matters when it engages a planet.
  • Idle stars are filtered out. A fixed star that is not involved in any paran with a planet is automatically dropped from the display, so you are not wading through stars that have nothing to say for this chart.
  • Results are grouped by orb. Tighter coincidences are separated from looser ones, so the strongest parans stand out.

Note

The paran and primary-direction calculations are, by the maintainer's own account, somewhat idiosyncratic: the angular transit time of each body is used directly as a kind of primary motion, rather than rotating the primum mobile around fixed angular placements as classical primary directions are usually computed. It is a defensible approach, but not the conventional one — keep that in mind when comparing Zodiac's numbers with another program's.

docs.text:
