docs.title: Paran Latitude Bands & City Lookup
docs.text: A paran depends on latitude: two bodies that fall exactly on angles together at one place may miss each other, or coincide more sharply, at another. Zodiac uses this fact to offer a text-based astro-locality tool — a separate paranatellonta table that reaches beyond the chart's own locality to show where a given paran plays out differently.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Think of it as a text-based cousin of astrocartography. Rather than drawing lines across a map, the table lists cities and shows, for a chosen paran, where that coincidence is more or less acute. A paran that is loose at your birthplace might be tight a few hundred miles north; this table lets you find those places.

The practical use is relocation-flavored: it helps you find places where you might want to seek a favorable paran, or avoid an unwelcome one, without casting a chart for every candidate city by hand.

the paran latitude-band table listing cities and their in-orb paran output for a chosen paran, for a neutral demo chart

docs.title: How the lookup works
docs.text:
The tool draws on Zodiac's built-in city database for its paran-latitude lookup, so it works offline without needing an online geocoding service. For each paran it reports the in-orb latitude band — the range of latitudes over which the coincidence holds — and the cities that fall within it, with clearer formatting for the band output.

Meridional parans are excluded

Parans formed only on the meridian — MC-MC, MC-IC, and IC-IC — are left out of this table. Meridian contacts are far less location-specific than horizon contacts (the meridian passage of a body barely depends on where you stand along a parallel), so including them would add rows that say little about place. Horizon-based parans, which shift meaningfully with latitude, are what this table is for.

docs.title: Locations and the city database
docs.text:
Because this feature is built on the same locality data the rest of the program uses, it is worth knowing how Zodiac resolves places, coordinates, and time zones. That is covered under Locations, time & calendars.

See also: Paranatellonta  ·  The Speculum  ·  Locations, time & calendars

docs.title: Paranatellonta
docs.text: Paranatellonta — parans — can be searched for over a span of time, the same way you search for transits or stations. Zodiac then gives you a dedicated paran chart for inspecting a given coincidence by eye, with a bi-wheel display mode built specifically to make angular coincidences easy to see.

docs.title: Finding paran events over a range
docs.text:
Paran finding lives in the Events panel, alongside the other event types. Enable paranatellonta events from the event-filter toolbar, set a date range, and Zodiac lists the paran events that fall inside it — each with the bodies involved, the angles they occupy, and its worked-out timing. As with any event, clicking a row brings the moment up on the chart so you can study it.

the Events panel with paranatellonta events enabled in the filter toolbar and a list of dated paran events for a neutral demo chart

Transit-to-natal parans are supported: the moving sky can form a paran against the positions of the birth chart, not only against itself. This lets you track when a transit brings a body onto an angle in coincidence with a natal body.

docs.title: The paran chart
docs.text:
For close visual inspection, Zodiac provides a dedicated paran chart UI. It is built around the fact that a paran is about where bodies sit relative to the angles at a single instant, so the display is arranged to make those angular placements plain rather than burying them in a conventional ecliptic wheel.

the dedicated paran chart for a single paran event, showing the two bodies sitting on their respective angles

docs.title: The bi-wheel prime-vertical display
docs.text:
The most useful view for parans is the bi-wheel prime-vertical (PV) display mode. In this mode the two charts of a bi-wheel are properly coordinated — they share a common reference frame — so a body genuinely on the horizon or meridian appears on the horizon or meridian, without the distortion you get from reading angular position off an ecliptic wheel. Because parans are precisely about bodies sitting on angles at the same moment, this coordinated PV view is especially well suited to visualizing them: two bodies in paran line up visibly against the frame.

The prime-vertical frame, and how it differs from the ecliptic, equatorial, and great-circle frames, is covered under Prime vertical, equatorial & great-circle.

a bi-wheel in prime-vertical mode with two bodies in paran aligned against the horizon/meridian frame

docs.title: Midpoints as paran participants
docs.text:
A paran chain need not be limited to whole bodies. Zodiac allows synthetic midpoint participants in a paran chain — a midpoint between two bodies can itself take part in the coincidence, positioned on the chart wheel from the chord midpoint. This extends paran searching to the midpoint structures that matter in harmonic and sidereal work.

See also: The Speculum  ·  Primary directions & quotidian modes  ·  Paran latitude bands & city lookup

docs.title: Primary Directions & Quotidian Modes
docs.text: Primary directions are one of the oldest timing techniques in astrology, and Zodiac generates them as tables you can read alongside a chart. This page explains the idea in plain terms and describes the direction methods Zodiac offers.

docs.title: What a primary direction is
docs.text:
Everything in the sky appears to turn once a day: bodies rise in the east, culminate at the meridian, set in the west, and pass the lower meridian, carried by the daily rotation of the earth. This daily turning is the primary motion (also called diurnal motion). In a primary direction, the angles and planets of a chart are "directed" by this motion — you let the sky keep turning and watch for the moment a promise in the chart is brought to perfection, such as an angle arriving at a planet or star.

The measurement is made in right ascension (position along the celestial equator, which is what the diurnal rotation actually sweeps through), and the arc of that motion is converted into time by a rate: as a rough rule, 1° of arc corresponds to about one year of life. Several rate conventions exist — the Naibod rate is a common one — and they differ slightly in how many years a degree buys, which is why two programs can report neighboring but not identical dates for the same direction.

Note

Zodiac's parans are timed with exactly this machinery: each paran's effective date is the moment the directed angle-as-significator meets the other body. That is why the Speculum can tell you, on hover, when a body's mundane primary direction comes into play.

docs.title: The tables Zodiac generates
docs.text:
Mundane primary directions. For a chart, Zodiac produces a mundane primary-directions table — directions worked in the mundane (angular) frame rather than by zodiacal degree.

PSSR for return charts. For solar-return charts — including demi- and quarter-returns — Zodiac instead generates PSSR (Progressed Sidereal Solar Return) timing, a return-based directional scheme. See Returns for how those charts are cast.

the mundane primary-directions table in the Tables view for a neutral demo chart, with effective dates shown

docs.title: Direction methods (quotidian modes)
docs.text:
The directional method is resolved per chart, and four modes are available, all from the solar-quotidian family:

  • SQ — solar quotidian.
  • NeoSQ — the "Neo" variant of SQ.
  • PSSR — Progressed Sidereal Solar Return.
  • NeoPSSR — the "Neo" variant of PSSR.

The distinction between the plain and "Neo" variants is which Sun they reference: the Neo variants use the apparent Sun's right ascension rather than the mean Sun's. That choice shifts the timing slightly and can be selected to match the convention you prefer.

docs.title: Including natal planets in a bi-wheel
docs.text:
When you build the primary-directions or PSSR table for the second chart of a bi-wheel, you can optionally have it include the natal planets as well, using their ex-precessed equatorial positions — so the directions of the return (or other second chart) can be read against the birth positions in one table.

the PSSR directions table for the second chart of a bi-wheel, with the option to include the natal planets enabled

See also: The Speculum  ·  Returns  ·  Paranatellonta

docs.title: The Speculum
docs.text:
A speculum is a table of angular timings. For each planet and each fixed star, it lists when that body rises, culminates (crosses the upper meridian), sets, and anti-culminates (crosses the lower meridian). Because a paran is simply two bodies on angles at the same instant, a speculum is the natural place to spot parans — the coincidences line up as matching times down the columns.

the Speculum dock listing each body's rising, MC, setting and IC times for a neutral demo chart

docs.title: Display modes
docs.text:
Each entry can be shown in one of three modes:

  • Right Ascension — the body's position on the equator, in degrees.
  • Sidereal Time — the local sidereal time of the angular contact.
  • Local Time — the clock time of the contact.

The mode syncs with the Tables view: change the display mode there and the Speculum follows, so the two stay consistent. (The Speculum lives among the text tables — see the Tables (text) view.)

docs.title: Reading and using the table
docs.text:
The Speculum is interactive, and this is where much of its value lies:

  • Hover over an entry to see when its mundane primary direction comes into play — that is, the timing at which the angle acting as significator reaches that body. This is the bridge between the static angular table and a date in a life; the underlying method is described under Primary directions & quotidian modes.
  • Click an entry to filter the display to every body that forms a paran with that body's angle transit. Instead of scanning the whole table by eye, you pick one angular contact and Zodiac shows you exactly which other bodies coincide with it.

docs.title: Working with cells
docs.text:
The Speculum supports the conveniences you would expect of a table:

  • Copy the selected cells with Ctrl+C.
  • Extended selection — select a range of cells to copy several timings at once.
  • A dedicated paran-orb setting governs how close two angular contacts must be to count as a paran, so you can tighten or loosen what the click-to-filter and paran displays treat as a coincidence.

Tip

The paran-orb setting and the radix-anchored clustering are shared between the Speculum and the directions tables, so a paran you tighten in one place stays consistent in the other.

See also: Tables (text) view  ·  Primary directions & quotidian modes  ·  Paranatellonta

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
The pages in this section are the ones you reach for to look something up rather than to learn a feature — the settings, the switches, and what to do when something goes wrong.

  • Settings Reference — a walk through the Settings dialog and its tabs: General, Chart, Tables, Events, and Harmonics.
  • Themes — the Dark, Light, and Printable themes and how they affect the whole interface.
  • Command-Line Options — flags for starting a fresh session or loading a specific one, and for running more than one instance.
  • Troubleshooting & Crash Reports — common setup snags, where your files live, and how crash reports are gathered.
  • Credits & License — the people, libraries, and license behind Zodiac.

docs.title: Command-Line Options
docs.text:
Zodiac normally runs as a single instance: launching it again while it is already open just raises the existing window. When you want a fresh workspace, or a specific session, or more than one instance running at once, start the program with one of these flags.

Option What it does --new Start a fresh session without restoring your previous state. Also accepted as -new and /new. --load-session <file> Launch with a specific session file (a .zos file).

Both options allow multiple concurrent instances — so you can, for example, keep your main workspace open and start a second, empty one with --new, or open a saved research session alongside it with --load-session.

Tip

You do not need the command line for everyday multi-window work. Double-clicking a .zos file opens that session, and right-clicking a session in the database offers Open in New Window. See Sessions & Multi-Window for those routes.

docs.title: The program
docs.text: Zodiac began as an open-source charting application by Artem Vasilev. This sidereal branch has been developed by Josh Baudhuin since 2016, adding the sidereal ayanamshas, harmonic search, parans and primary directions, the event engine, and the session and database features described throughout this guide.

docs.title: Built on
docs.text:
Zodiac stands on the work of others:

  • Swiss Ephemeris — the astronomical library that provides the planetary and house calculations.
  • The Qt framework — the cross-platform toolkit the application's interface is built with.
  • The Almagest and DejaVu fonts — used for astrological glyphs and text throughout the program.

docs.title: Settings Reference
docs.text: The Settings dialog is where you tune how Zodiac calculates and displays charts. It is organized into tabs — General, Chart, Tables, Events, and Harmonics — each grouping a related set of options. Your choices persist across sessions, so what you set here is what you get next time you open the program.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
The General tab holds the program-wide preferences:

  • Theme — choose the Dark, Light, or Printable look (see Themes).
  • Ask about unsaved files — whether Zodiac prompts you before closing a chart that has unsaved changes.
  • Timezone & Geography API — the Google API key and endpoint used to look up the latitude, longitude, and time zone of places you enter. Location search needs a valid key; see Locations, time & calendars.
  • Show age — whether a person's age is displayed alongside their chart.
  • Default location — the place used for new charts and for transit searches when you have not specified one.

The tab also has the usual controls for saving the current values as your defaults, restoring the built-in defaults, and OK / Cancel to apply or discard your changes.

the Settings dialog open on the General tab, showing the theme selector, the unsaved-files and show-age checkboxes, the Timezone and Geography API key field, the default location, and the Save as Defaults / By default / OK / Cancel / Apply buttons

docs.title: Chart
docs.text:
The Chart tab governs how the chart wheel is drawn — the display options for the wheel itself, such as what is shown around and inside it.

the Settings dialog open on the Chart tab

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
The Tables tab governs the text (Tables) view — the options for how chart information is presented in tables rather than on the wheel.

the Settings dialog open on the Tables tab

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
The Events tab holds the defaults for event filtering and search — the starting points the Events panel uses before you adjust them per tab.

the Settings dialog open on the Events tab

docs.title: Harmonics
docs.text:
The Harmonics tab governs the display and scope of harmonics — controls such as the minimum and maximum quorum, and the orbs used when gathering harmonic patterns.

the Settings dialog open on the Harmonics tab

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
Zodiac ships with three themes, so you can match the program to how and where you are working:

  • Dark (default) — a low-glare look tuned for comfortable viewing, including at night.
  • Light — a clean, high-contrast interface for bright rooms and daytime work.
  • Printable — an ink-saving black-and-gray variant, based on the light theme, for when you want to print a chart or a table without pouring toner into a dark background.

A theme applies to the whole interface, not just one panel — the menus, toolbars, and docks, the chart rendering on the wheel, the HTML output of the Plain and Details views, and the tables. Everything switches together, so the program stays consistent whichever theme you choose.

Your choice persists across sessions: set it once and Zodiac remembers it the next time you launch.

docs.title: Switching themes
docs.text:
Change the theme from the General tab of the Settings dialog — see the Settings Reference. The interface updates as soon as you apply the change, so you can see the effect immediately.

the same demo chart shown in the Dark theme the same demo chart shown in the Light theme, for side-by-side comparison with the Dark version above

Tip

Reach for the Printable theme just before printing or exporting a chart or table. It keeps the layout intact while dropping the dark fills that would otherwise waste ink.

docs.title: Troubleshooting & Crash Reports
docs.text: Most problems with Zodiac fall into one of two buckets: a setup step that hasn't been completed, or the rare unexpected close. This page covers both, and tells you where your files live so you can find, back up, or move them.

docs.title: Location search doesn't work
docs.text: The single most common setup snag is location lookup. Zodiac uses a Google geography and time-zone service to turn a place name into coordinates and a time zone, and that service needs an API key. If searching for a city returns nothing, the key is usually missing or invalid. Without a key, Zodiac starts on its offline city database instead, which covers towns and cities but may miss very small places. See Locations, time & calendars for how to supply the key and confirm it is working.

docs.title: Crash reports
docs.text:
If Zodiac closes unexpectedly, a release build captures a crash report — a minidump plus a symbolized stack trace — and saves it under:

%LOCALAPPDATA%\Zodiac\crashes

The next time you launch the program, you are offered the chance to bundle the report into a single zip file and reveal it in the file manager, ready to send on. Gathering that zip is the most useful first step if you want to report a crash, because the symbolized stack tells the maintainer where the problem occurred.

docs.title: Where your files live
docs.text:
Knowing these locations helps with backups, cloud sync, and moving to a new machine:

  • Charts — in your Documents folder, typically Documents/zodiac-charts.
  • Sessions — .zos files in the same user documents area (see Sessions & Multi-Window).
  • Settings — kept in your user directory so they persist across sessions.
  • Crash reports — %LOCALAPPDATA%\Zodiac\crashes, as above.

Tip

Because charts and sessions both live in your Documents folder, backing them up (or syncing them through OneDrive or another cloud service) is just a matter of including that folder. See The Chart Database.

docs.title: The Views
docs.text:
The same chart can be shown in more than one way. Zodiac gives you four views of a single open chart, and you switch between them freely without recasting anything: a classical chart wheel, a Planets view, a Tables (text) view, and a Details view. Each shows the same underlying data from a different angle — a picture, a focused look at the planets, plain text tables, or detailed properties of one element.

Crucially, the display options that shape what you see — the harmonic, the house system, the zodiac, the aspect set, and the aspect mode (ecliptic, prime vertical, equatorial, or great-circle) — are treated as view-level settings, not properties of the chart file. Switching them changes what is drawn without marking the chart dirty, so you can experiment with display options and never be prompted to save a change you did not really make.

docs.title: The four views
docs.text:
• The Chart Wheel — the default view; a classical wheel of signs, houses, planets, and aspect lines.
  • Planets Panel — a dockable table of every body's position for one or two charts, with a search that finds a chart from typed positions.
  • Tables (Text) View — the chart's information as text tables in lieu of the wheel.
  • Details — detailed properties and interpretations for a selected element.

The wheel has many capabilities of its own; those are gathered in The Chart Wheel in Depth.

docs.title: The Chart Wheel
docs.text:
The chart wheel is Zodiac's default view and the one you will spend the most time with. It is a classical wheel: the zodiac ring around the outside, the houses divided within it, and the planets placed at their positions, all drawn from the Swiss Ephemeris.

At a glance the wheel shows you:

  • The signs and houses — the zodiac ring and the house divisions for the house system currently selected.
  • The planets, laid out with their glyphs at their chart positions.
  • Aspect lines between the planets, with aspect intensity shown by line thickness — a tighter, stronger aspect draws a heavier line, so the most significant contacts stand out.
  • Fixed stars near planets — stars that fall within close direct (great-circle) distance of a planet are shown on the wheel.
  • Midpoint chords — midpoint structures are drawn as chord lines between the planets involved.
the chart wheel as the central view for a neutral demo chart — zodiac ring, house divisions, planet glyphs, and aspect lines of varying thickness across the center

docs.title: There is much more to the wheel
docs.text:
The wheel is far more capable than this quick tour suggests. It can be redrawn for any harmonic from H1 to H32, switched between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs, shown in different coordinate frames (prime vertical, equatorial, great-circle), paired with a declination strip, and animated through time.

All of those capabilities have their own section:

The Chart Wheel in Depth →

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The Details view displays detailed properties and interpretations for a single selected element — a planet or another chart element — rather than the chart as a whole. Where the other views show the entire horoscope, this one goes deep on one thing at a time: select an element and the view fills with its properties and the relevant interpretive text.

It draws from the same open chart as the other views, so nothing is recast when you switch to it. Its output is rendered as theme-aware HTML, so it follows the current Dark, Light, or Printable theme and stays readable on screen and in print.

the Details view for a neutral demo chart, showing the detailed properties and interpretation text for one selected planet

Note

For the planets as a group rather than one element in depth, see the Planets view; for the chart's data as text tables you can copy, see the Tables (text) view.

docs.title: Planets Panel
docs.text:
The Planets panel is a dockable table listing where every body stands: the Ascendant and Midheaven first, then the Sun through Pluto, the nodes and any other bodies the chart carries. Open it from the panels menu like the Details, Events and Speculum panels.

When a second chart is loaded (a transit, progression, return…), its positions appear in a Chart 2 column beside the first, so the two can be read across row by row. Positions are ecliptic longitudes in the zodiac the tab is displaying, written with the sign's glyph; an R marks a retrograde body.

Further columns give chart 1's declination, right ascension, mundane position (round the circle of the current direction system, 0° at the Ascendant) and house. Right-click the column headings to choose which of them to show.

Click a row to select that planet in the other panels. Select cells and press Ctrl+C to copy them (positions are copied with the sign's abbreviation).

docs.title: Finding a chart from its positions
docs.text:
Press Search to turn the table into a search form. This is meant for recovering a chart from positions alone — a horoscope printed in an old book, or a modern chart whose date you want to establish.

  1. Tick the bodies whose positions you know. A ticked row is part of the search, and its position becomes editable: type over it with any of 15 Leo, 15°23' Leo, 15Le23, Leo 15 23, or an absolute longitude such as 135.4. What you type is rewritten the way the table writes positions (9 Can 51 becomes 9°51' Can), to the precision you gave and no further. Tab and Enter move on to the next ticked row. Unticked rows are ignored and simply go on showing the open chart.

    When only the sign is known, type the sign by itself (Leo). The body may then stand anywhere in that sign, and the Orb is how far past the sign's edges still counts. 2. Choose the Zodiac the positions are given in. It starts out matching the tab but is independent of it: you can search for a tropical chart while the wheel shows a sidereal one. While searching, the whole table is shown in this zodiac. 3. Set the Orb — how far a body may stand from what you typed. Printed charts given to the whole degree want at least 1°. 4. Set the range of Years to look through. Years use astronomical numbering (0 is 1 BC). 5. Press Find.

Matches are listed best fit first. Select one — by clicking, or with the arrow keys — to show it. Where it goes depends on what is open:

  • beside chart 1, as chart 2, when chart 1 is a person, event, return or composite chart;
  • in place of chart 1 when it is any other kind of chart (a new untitled chart, say) — the positions the search took from it are kept as if typed;
  • in a tab of its own when no chart is open.

Stepping through the list re-points that same chart, and the search is left as it was. Double-click or middle-click a match to open it in a new tab, as that tab's chart 1, to keep.

A row you tick but do not type over stands for the open chart's own position. The tick box at the top of the column ticks or unticks every row at once, so ticking it and pressing Find looks for the chart you already have open — the quickest way to try the search out. Unticking a row puts the chart's value back.

When nothing matches

Tables before the modern era were often degrees off for Mercury and Mars. Raise Misses to let one or two bodies fall outside the orb, or widen the orb.

docs.title: What the angles add
docs.text:
Planets alone fix the date; the Moon fixes the time to within a few hours. The Ascendant and Midheaven do more, in one of two ways:

  • Without a known place, the Midheaven gives the chart's local mean time directly, and Ascendant and Midheaven together give the latitude. The longitude is the difference between that local time and Universal Time, and UT comes from the bodies — in practice the Moon. The Earth turns 27 times faster than the Moon moves, so any vagueness in the Moon's position is magnified 27-fold in the longitude: a Moon given to the whole degree leaves it uncertain by about ±14°, one given to the minute by about ±0.5°. The uncertainty shown beside each value follows from how precisely you stated the positions (and widens if they disagree with one another by more than that); the Orb only decides whether a chart counts as a match.

A place is suggested from the result: the nearest city when the position is closely fixed, otherwise the largest one within the uncertainty. The notes of the opened chart say how far the solved position lies from it. For dates from 1900 the Zone column gives the clock time that place kept, and the chart opens in that zone time rather than local mean time — check any daylight-saving time against a historical source. - With "Known place" ticked, the angles are used the other way round: they pin the time of day to within minutes, and the Moon becomes a check on it.

The Ascendant by itself needs either a Midheaven or a known place.

docs.title: Charts given by sign
docs.text:
Old horoscopes often give no more than the sign each body stood in and the sign that was rising. Type the signs alone, tick Known place and enter the place the chart is thought to come from — it cannot be worked out from a rising sign.

Seven bodies by sign normally single out one stretch of a day or two in many centuries. The rising sign then narrows each day of that stretch to the two hours or so during which it was on the Ascendant, so there is one match per day. The UT column gives the middle of the span and its half-length (14:58 ±1h); nothing in the data says where within it the chart falls. If the Moon or another body is known to the degree, the days reduce to one.

Note

For the chart's data as text tables you can copy — with rulerships, aspects and more — see the Tables (Text) view. For the properties of a single planet, see Details.

docs.title: Tables (Text) View
docs.text:
The Tables (text) view shows the chart's information as text tables in place of the wheel. It is the view to reach for when you want to read the numbers, compare values row by row, or copy data out — everything the wheel expresses as a picture, laid out as text.

For a given chart it can present:

  • Positions — the planets' positions.
  • House rulerships — which planets rule which houses.
  • Aspects — the aspects in the chart.
  • The Speculum — rising, culmination, setting, and anti-culmination data for the bodies (see The Speculum).
  • Primary Directions and PSSR directions — mundane primary-direction timings, and Primary Solar/Sidereal Return timings for return charts (see Primary directions & quotidian modes).
  • Parans — the paranatellonta tables.

docs.title: Display mode
docs.text: A display-mode control switches how times and positions are expressed between Local Time, Sidereal Time, and Right Ascension. This control is kept in sync with the Speculum dock, so changing the mode in one place updates the other.

docs.title: Showing and hiding sections
docs.text: Because the view can hold a lot of material at once, compact per-section toggles (the SectionToggle controls in the toolbar) let you show or hide individual sections — turn off the tables you are not using and keep only what you want to read.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: The view's output is theme-aware: it follows the current Dark, Light, or Printable theme, so the tables stay readable on screen and print cleanly.
